los.text: Identify the rostral/anterior, caudal/posterior, inferior/ventral and superior/dorsal aspects of the brain and spinal cord
los.html:
TermSpinal cord and brainstemCerebrum (forebrain)
RostralSuperior (towards the head)Anterior (towards the nose)
CaudalInferiorPosterior (towards the occiput)
DorsalPosteriorSuperior (top of the head)
VentralAnteriorInferior (base of brain)
  • Why they differ: the neuraxis bends about 90° at the junction of midbrain and diencephalon, so "dorsal" means posterior in the cord but superior in the cerebrum.

los.text: Identify the grey and white matter of the brain and spinal cord
los.html:
Grey matterNeuronal cell bodies, dendrites and synapses (processing). White matter: myelinated axon tracts (conduction); white because of myelin.
Brain
  • Grey on the outside (cerebral and cerebellar cortex) plus deep grey nuclei (basal ganglia, thalamus)
  • White matter inside (corona radiata, internal capsule, corpus callosum).
Spinal cordThe reverse: grey inside (H/butterfly: dorsal horn sensory, ventral horn motor, lateral horn T1–L2 sympathetic) and white outside (dorsal, lateral, ventral columns).
MRIT1: white matter brighter than grey, CSF dark. T2: CSF bright, grey brighter than white.

los.text: Identify the cerebral hemispheres, corpus callosum, midbrain, pons, medulla, cerebellum, ventricles, thalamus, basal ganglia and hypothalamus on a 3D model/prosection of the brain and on MRI brain scans
los.html:
StructureWhereFunction
Cerebral hemispheresLargest part, two halvesCortex: movement, sensation, language, cognition
Corpus callosumMidline white matter bridgeLinks the two hemispheres
ThalamusEither side of the 3rd ventricleRelay of all senses (except smell) to cortex; motor loops; arousal
HypothalamusBelow thalamus, floor of 3rd ventricleHomeostasis: temperature, hunger, thirst, sleep, autonomic and pituitary control
Basal gangliaDeep grey nuclei (caudate, putamen, globus pallidus)Starting and smoothing movement (Parkinson's, Huntington's)
MidbrainTop of brainstemCN III and IV, eye movements, pupil reflexes, substantia nigra, cerebral aqueduct
PonsMiddle of brainstem, bulging forwardsCN V–VIII, relays cortex to cerebellum, breathing rhythm
MedullaLowest brainstem, to foramen magnumCN IX–XII, cardiovascular and respiratory centres, pyramids (corticospinal decussation)
CerebellumPosterior cranial fossaCoordination, balance, motor learning (same side)
  • Ventricles and CSF: lateral ventricles
    • → interventricular foramen
    • → 3rd ventricle
    • → cerebral aqueduct
    • → 4th ventricle
    • → median and lateral apertures
    • → subarachnoid space
    • made by choroid plexus (~500 mL/day), absorbed by arachnoid granulations into the venous sinuses.

los.text: Recognise the anatomy of a typical spinal nerve as exemplified by a thoracic spinal nerve, including its origin from the dorsal and ventral spinal roots
los.html:
Dorsal rootSensory; cell bodies in the dorsal root ganglion (pseudounipolar).
Ventral rootMotor (ventral horn); at T1–L2 also preganglionic sympathetic fibres (lateral horn).
Spinal nerveThe two roots join in the intervertebral foramen → a short mixed nerve.
Dorsal ramus
  • Deep back muscles and skin of the back.
  • Ventral ramus: in the thorax, the intercostal nerve (anterolateral wall muscles and skin).
Rami communicantesWhite (preganglionic, myelinated, T1–L2 only) to the sympathetic trunk; grey (postganglionic) back to every spinal nerve.
Count
  • 31 pairs (8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, 1 coccygeal)
  • C1–7 exit above their vertebra, C8 below C7, all others below theirs.

los.text: Recognise the parts of the developing nervous system and the processes involved in its development
los.html:
Neurulation (weeks 3–4)
  • Notochord induces ectoderm
  • → neural plate
  • → neural folds and groove
  • → folds fuse into the neural tube (starts mid-embryo ~day 22; cranial neuropore closes ~day 25, caudal ~day 28).
Neural tubeBrain and spinal cord; its lumen → ventricles and central canal.
Neural crest(from the fold edges)Dorsal root and autonomic ganglia, Schwann cells, adrenal medulla, melanocytes, enteric neurons, pia and arachnoid, much of the face skeleton.
Primary vesicle (week 4)Secondary vesicle (week 5)Becomes
ProsencephalonTelencephalonCerebral hemispheres
DiencephalonThalamus, hypothalamus, retina and optic nerve
MesencephalonMesencephalonMidbrain
RhombencephalonMetencephalonPons, cerebellum
MyelencephalonMedulla
PlatesAlar (dorsal) = sensory; basal (ventral) = motor; divided by the sulcus limitans.
DefectsAnencephaly (cranial neuropore fails); spina bifida (caudal: occulta, meningocele, myelomeningocele); raised AFP; folic acid prevents many.

los.text: Identify the frontal, parietal, temporal and occipital lobes
los.html:
LobeBoundariesKey areas and functions
FrontalIn front of the central sulcus, above the lateral sulcusPrimary motor cortex (precentral gyrus), planning, personality, Broca's area (speech output, dominant side), frontal eye fields
ParietalCentral sulcus to parieto-occipital sulcusPrimary somatosensory cortex (postcentral gyrus), spatial awareness (neglect if non-dominant), reading, writing, calculation
TemporalBelow the lateral (Sylvian) sulcusPrimary auditory cortex, Wernicke's area (comprehension), memory (hippocampus), smell, upper visual field fibres (Meyer's loop)
OccipitalBehind the parieto-occipital sulcusPrimary visual cortex around the calcarine sulcus

los.text: Identify and list the anatomical components of the central nervous system, peripheral nervous system and the autonomic nervous system
los.html:
SystemParts
CNSBrain (cerebrum, diencephalon, brainstem, cerebellum) and spinal cord; meninges (dura, arachnoid, pia) and CSF; glia: astrocytes, oligodendrocytes (myelin), microglia, ependyma
PNS12 cranial nerves (optic is really CNS), 31 spinal nerves, plexuses, ganglia; Schwann cells myelinate
ANS
  • Sympathetic (thoracolumbar, T1–L2; short pre-, long postganglionic; noradrenaline)
  • Parasympathetic (craniosacral: III, VII, IX, X and S2–4; long pre-, short postganglionic; acetylcholine)
  • Enteric (myenteric and submucosal plexuses)

los.text: Identify the components of a spinal reflex arc and recognise the significance of enhanced and absent tendon reflexes
los.html:
1. ReceptorMuscle spindle senses stretch (tendon tap).
2. AfferentIa sensory neuron, cell body in the dorsal root ganglion.
3. IntegrationSynapse in the spinal cord (stretch reflex is monosynaptic).
4. Efferentα motor neuron from the ventral horn.
5. EffectorThe same muscle contracts.
Absent or reduceda lower motor neuron problem: a break anywhere in the arc (neuropathy, root compression, anterior horn disease, muscle disease; also spinal shock early on).
BriskAn upper motor neuron lesion (stroke, MS, cord compression above that level): lost descending inhibition, with clonus, spasticity and an up-going plantar.
ReinforcementClenching the teeth or pulling the hands apart (Jendrassik) brings out a weak reflex.

los.text: Identify the spinal root values of the five main reflexes (biceps, brachioradialis, triceps, knee and ankle)
los.html:
ReflexRoot value
BicepsC5, C6
Brachioradialis (supinator)C5, C6 (mainly C6)
TricepsC7 (C6–8)
KneeL3, L4
AnkleS1 (S1–2)
  • Rhyme: "S1, 2 buckle my shoe; 3, 4 kick the door; 5, 6 pick up sticks; 7, 8 lay them straight."
